svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Two standard fixes that expired, and one problem that arrived
svg.desc: Three panels. The advice to disable the newer address family has expired, because it now carries more than half of measured traffic, some networks are reachable only that way, and disabling it breaks connectivity while the correct fix is a tunnel that carries or blocks it at the interface. The advice to disable browser real time communication has largely expired, because browsers adopted an obfuscation scheme in 2019 that closed the local address half by default, while disabling the feature breaks video calling. A new problem arrived instead: browsers now perform their own encrypted name resolution by default, and the browser's chosen resolver takes priority over the one the tunnel configured. A band below observes that leak fixes age faster than leaks.
svg.text: Figure 3: Two Fixes That Expired, One Problem That Arrived
The leaks in this lesson are mostly unchanged. The remedies attached to them have moved, and two are now worse than the problem.

g.text: Why it was reasonable
Many tunnels carried only the older
address family, so the newer one went
around them silently.
Why it is not any more
It passed half of measured global
traffic in March 2026. Some mobile
networks and modern data centres are
reachable only that way, and
translation gateways depend on it.
What to do instead
Use a tunnel that either carries it or
blocks it at the interface. Both are
correct. Turning it off system-wide is
a change to everything you do.
Why it was reasonable
The feature discovered and reported
both your local address and your public
one to any page that asked.
What changed
Browsers adopted an obfuscation scheme
in 2019 that replaces the local address
with a random name. That half is closed
by default on major desktop browsers.
The public address goes through the
tunnel when routing is correct.
What to do instead
Test it rather than assume. Disabling
the feature outright breaks video
calling, which people then re-enable.
What happens
Browsers now perform their own
encrypted name resolution, on by
default in several regions.
Why it matters here
The browser's chosen resolver takes
priority over the one your tunnel
configured. Your lookups are encrypted
and they go to somebody the tunnel
did not pick.
Is it a leak?
Not in the old sense: your network
operator still cannot read it. But you
no longer know who is answering, which
is a different question worth asking.

svg.text: The pattern, which is the transferable part

g.text: Leaks are stable and remedies are not. The six mechanisms in Figure 1 have barely changed in a decade. The advice attached to them has changed completely.
Two of these remedies now cost more than the leak. Turning off half the internet, or breaking video calls, to close a gap that was closed for you five years ago.
Copied guidance never notices. These instructions propagate between articles without anybody rechecking whether the underlying situation still holds.
So test the leak, and separately ask whether the fix is still the fix. Those are two different pieces of work and only the first one gets done.

svg.text: This is the same failure Lesson 5.2 described for application recommendations, arriving in a technical setting where it looks more authoritative.
A checklist that tells you to disable something is making a claim about the present. Date it, or the claim outlives the reason for it.
And notice that the newly arrived item was nobody's misconfiguration. It was a decision made about your traffic by somebody else.
